 Senate Democrats united in support of El-Sayed, minority leader says
 By Elise Hammond 
 Minority Leader Chuck Schumer reiterated Senate Democrats’ support for Abdul El-Sayed after his Democratic primary opponent broke with the party and endorsed the Republican nominee in Michigan’s critical race.
 “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” Schumer said in a statement.
 Schumer also called the “racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks” targeted at El-Sayed “evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.”

 Stevens' move to endorse Rogers blindsides staffers and longtime friends, sources say
 By Jeff Zeleny 
 Rep. Haley Stevens attends the Lansing Regional Chamber of Commerce "Meet the Candidate" series in Lansing, Michigan, on July 29. 
 Bill Pugliano/Getty Images 
 Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens’ decision to appear with — and later endorse — Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers today blindsided several of her staffers, outside political advisers and longtime Democratic friends, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
 One person who has spoken to Stevens every day this week called her behavior “a complete and embarrassing betrayal.”
 While some of Stevens’ staffers have already started looking for work or left her office, given her term in Congress ends in two months, others submitted their resignations today.
 Stevens, who has long been seen as a team player inside the world of Michigan politics, had increasingly stopped taking advice from her longtime allies. She is relying on the counsel of her fiancé, Jason Turkish, a lawyer who had already endorsed Rogers, people familiar with the matter tell CNN.
 “She’s taking cues from Jason and blowing up her relationships with Michigan Democrats,” one person who has spoken to Stevens multiple times this week told CNN.

 Stevens says she was not welcomed by El-Sayed campaign
 By Maureen Chowdhury 
 Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens repeatedly said that Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed did not want her to be a part of his campaign as she explained her decision to endorse his Republican rival today.
 “Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn’t need me there, that he didn’t want me there, and at some point, you got to look at who’s standing for country,” Stevens, a moderate Democrat, said as she stood alongside GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers outside a Detroit church Sunday.
 Stevens said she’s been a Democrat for a long time and that she “meant it” when she endorsed El-Sayed earlier this year.
 “But Abdul was very clear. He said, ‘Don’t come.’ I endorsed him. I meant it when I endorsed him. I gave him a big hug. I stood there. I was just having a good time. I love volunteering on campaigns, and when it really comes down to it, this is how I’m passing my ballot,” Stevens said. “It’s going to be a close election, and everyone can take a look at the facts.”

 Rogers and Stevens conclude remarks after individual shouts "Haley's a traitor"

 Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers speaks during a press conference with Rep. Haley Stevens in Detroit on Sunday.

 Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens and Republican Mike Rogers stopped taking questions from reporters on Sunday after an individual in the crowd outside a Detroit church shouted, “Haley’s a traitor.”
 Stevens’ move to endorse Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, her former primary rival, in the critical Senate race has quickly drawn outrage in the Democratic world, with CNN reporting that her chief of staff and communications director have resigned.

 “We can’t stand with hate,” Stevens says after endorsing Rogers
 By Maureen Chowdhury 
 “We can’t stand with hate,” Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens said following her endorsement of GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers.
 “My vote for Senate is going to be with Mike Rogers, and I will tell you why. Because we have to stand with country. We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker,” she said during remarks to reporters after she attended a service with Rogers at Perfecting Church in Detroit.
 Stevens said that while she has not cast her ballot yet, “90% of the votes I’m going to cast are going to be for Democrats.”

 Michigan Democrats rebuke Stevens' decision to campaign with GOP Senate nominee
 By Eric Bradner and Catherine Nicholls 
 Leaders from the Michigan Democratic Party swiftly rebuked Rep. Haley Stevens for appearing with Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in Detroit earlier today, with the organization’s chair saying she has “abandoned everything she claims to care about.”
 Stevens has since formally endorsed Rogers in a video posted to her X account.
 “Mike Rogers is Donald Trump’s hand-picked candidate for Senate, a rubber stamp for Trump’s toxic agenda, and a corrupt politician looking out only for himself,” Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said in a statement.
 “Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers—a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda—shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about,” Hertel continued, rejecting what he called Stevens’ attempts to “divide our party and undermine our momentum.”
 The state party’s First Vice Chair Portia Roberson said Stevens chose to spend this morning “in a Detroit church where the Republican candidate was making his pitch, rather than supporting the Democratic ticket.”
 “Any Democrat who has ever asked for OUR votes owes it to this community to stand clearly against him. Disagreements inside our party are settled at the ballot box, and they were. On Tuesday, Michigan Democrats are voting for Abdul El-Sayed,” Roberson said.
 DNC Black Caucus Chair Virgie Rollins slammed the endorsement and said the caucus is “dismayed that Congresswoman Haley Stevens has revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.” Rollins reiterated that the caucus is “proud to stand behind” El-Sayed.

 Haley Stevens breaks with her party to endorse Michigan Republican Senate nominee
 By Katherine Dautrich 
 Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens announced Sunday that she is endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race.
 While Stevens had initially said she would support progressive Abdul El Sayed, her former rival in the Democratic primary, she moved to back his opponent in the consequential Senate race after appearing with Rogers at a church on Sunday morning.
 “As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for US Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” Stevens, a moderate Democrat, said in a video posted to X.
 CNN and other outlets previously reported that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to stay away from his events despite them originally being scheduled to appear together at a church on Sunday.

 Neera Tanden slams Stevens for appearing with Rogers in Michigan
 By Katherine Koretski 
 Neera Tanden speaks during a rally on May 21, 2025, in Washington, DC. 
 Jemal Countess/Getty Images 
 Neera Tanden, a former Biden administration adviser who heads a Democratic think tank, is slamming Rep. Haley Stevens for appearing with Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in Detroit today.
 Standing with Rogers “is a betrayal of everything Haley Stevens has fought for her entire career. It’s also a betrayal of all of her supporters that believed in her,” Tanden wrote in a post on X .
 Tanden said she hopes Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed “has a strong victory on Tuesday and that all Democrats and like-minded independents support vote for him.”
 “Mike Rogers’ policies would not only hurt working class Michiganders but he’s run a disgusting, divisive campaign. That form of politics should be shunned, not embraced,” she added.
 Tanden, who serves as president and CEO at the Center for American Progress, has worked with Stevens in the past. She publicly doubted the viability of El-Sayed’s candidacy during the primary election, calling it a “risk” for him to take on Republicans in Michigan.

 Stevens appears with GOP Senate nominee in Michigan 
 1:11
 In a surprising move on a day that was supposed to be about unity for Democrats in Michigan, Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens is appearing with GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers in Detroit.
 “HAPPENING NOW: Congresswoman Haley Stevens joins Mike Rogers at church in Detroit this morning,” Rogers spokesperson Abby Ronson posted on X alongside a picture of the politicians.
 Across town, Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in a contentious primary this summer, will campaign with Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Stevens was supposed to appear with the Democrats, but the rift between the nominee and his former opponent appears to have deepened.
 Tensions rose this week after the announcement of the unity event. Stevens released a statement pressuring El-Sayed to condemn an ad made by an outside organization that blames Americans’ struggle with high costs on US aid to Israel.
 On Saturday, El-Sayed said he did not agree with the content of the ad, and Stevens later released a statement commending him for the move.
 But a Rogers campaign source told CNN that El-Sayed’s remarks Saturday minimizing the dispute pushed Stevens to appear with the Republican.
 “I just really don’t think any of this matters,” El-Sayed told reporters yesterday as he side-stepped questions from reporters on the unfolding drama, arguing that voters are more concerned with the cost of living than the dispute between the two Democrats.

 Warnock accuses Cruz of "bigotry" in comments about Muslims
 By Alison Main 
 Sen. Raphael Warnock speaks during a campaign event for New Hampshire Democratic Senate candidate Chris Pappas in Nashua, New Hampshire, October 6. 
 John Tully/Getty Images 
 Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock accused Sen. Ted Cruz of “bigotry” after the Texas Republican appeared to link the Muslim faith to terrorism during a final campaign sprint for GOP candidates ahead of Tuesday’s election.
 “It’s bigotry, pure and simple. Religious bigotry is bigotry, and the Republicans know that they’re losing the argument. It’s just deeply disheartening, though not terribly surprising that they’re trying to stir up these old demons,” he said on CNN’s “State of the Union.”
 On the campaign trail in Kansas’s competitive Senate race, Cruz responded to comments by Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, that people of the Muslim faith would be “welcomed in heaven.”
 “Interesting idea. We show up there in heaven, the first thing you see is Osama bin Laden,” Cruz retorted.
 Warnock, who is a Baptist minister, asserted “there is no religious test for citizenship in America, and there’s no religious test to hold office.”
 “As a Christian pastor, I take no comfort in this kind of Islamophobia and this kind of bigotry of lifting up the worst example of someone who claims a faith and trying to conflate that as to faith itself. As an African American, I know bigotry when I see it. We have to resist it, reject it. America is so much better than this,” he continued.
 CNN has reached out to Cruz’ office for comment.
 The Georgia Democrat also teased a potential presidential bid, saying, “come 2028, I will be running for high office.”
 Pressed by CNN’s Jake Tapper whether that office was the White House, Warnock, who is up for reelection in 2028, reiterated that he will be “running for high office,” adding, “yeah, a senator is a high office.”
 “I am very much focused on the midterms. If we don’t get 2026 right, seriously, we’re going to be in trouble. 2028 is theoretical,” he said.

 FBI instructs agents to steer clear of routine enforcement actions near voting sites
 By Josh Campbell 
 Some FBI leaders across the country are instructing their agents to avoid unrelated routine investigative actions around election polling sites as the 2026 midterms enter the final stretch, multiple sources tell CNN.
 While sources were unfamiliar with any nationwide guidance sent to all FBI employees from agency headquarters, some field office leaders have proactively reminded agents that federal law generally prohibits armed government agents from stationing themselves at polling sites and instructed personnel to refrain from conducting routine enforcement activity in the vicinity of voters casting ballots.
 On Saturday, the FBI’s Washington, DC, field office — which has agents assigned to patrol efforts as part of President Donald Trump’s crime prevention surge in the nation’s capital — sent many of its personnel similar guidance, noting FBI agents should avoid polling stations unless responding to an emergency such as reports of an active shooter.
 Sources say there remains notable anxiety across the FBI by many personnel who are fearful the organization will be thrust by the Trump administration into investigating baseless claims of election fraud in coming weeks.
 While the FBI has routinely advised its personnel in past election cycles to avoid polling sites, sources said the current guidance being shared by some field commanders is welcome in light of recent comments by the agency’s director , who wavered on the topic of sending FBI agents to polling places.
 Agents are still permitted to visit election sites to cast their own ballots.

 Beshear optimistic that Democrats could flip up to 6 governor's offices
 By Austin Culpepper 
 Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear speaks during an event with the South Carolina Democratic Party on October 2, in Santee, South Carolina. 
 Sean Rayford/Getty Images 
 Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear says Democrats could pick up as many as six governorships on election night. Beshear, who is the chair of the Democratic Governors Association, seemed optimistic about the party’s chances even in deep-red states.
 “It’s not just Texas; it’s Florida, it’s Nebraska, it’s Oklahoma, all of which are in the margin of error, so we are doing as much as we can in as many places as we can, and we’re really excited that we could pick up 4, 5, 6 governorships on November 3,” he told MS NOW on Sunday.
 Beshear also defended the DGA’s slow investment in state Rep. Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial campaign in Texas, calling it “one of the last states to become really competitive.”
 The Kentucky governor, who has openly toyed with a presidential run, left the door open for 2028.
 “I’m going to get through November 3. I’m hopefully going to get a little bit of sleep, celebrate with a whole lot of new governors, and then when I’m done being DGA chair, maybe take my family on vacation and we can have a conversation about it then,” he said.

 DNC chair says he expects lawsuits after Election Day: "We're prepared for that”
 By Katherine Koretski 
 Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said he is prepared for lawsuits after Election Day if Democrats are victorious, adding that President Donald Trump will do “anything he can” to keep Republicans in power.
 “Truly, and so we’re prepared for that. We’re prepared for all sorts of crazy chicanery after the election, and we’ll have to protect the outcome as much as we’re working to protect the vote,” Martin said in an interview on NewsNation Sunday.
 But Martin emphasizes he believes the election will be “free and fair.”
 “I believe we will have a free and fair election, but I do believe that there will be lawsuits after this election, and we’re prepared for that. And we’re prepared to protect not only the vote but protect the outcome of this election,” he added.
 This comes as the Justice Department has accelerated a criminal prob e into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a Senate candidate to siphon votes from the Republican candidate.

 Haley Stevens commends Abdul El-Sayed for denouncing ad
 By Katherine Koretski 
 Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. 
 Getty Images 
 Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens commended Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed for denouncing an outside group’s controversial ad about US aid to Israel, a topic that has loomed over his candidacy in recent days.
 “Michigan is at its best when we stand up for each other: Jewish families, Black congregations, Arab American neighbors, all of us,” Stevens said in a statement Saturday night. “I was glad to see our Senate nominee say he does not agree with the content of the vile Rebellion PAC ad, which claimed Israel and Jews were to blame for the high costs of groceries. Whenever anyone tries to set us against each other, we have an obligation to stand up and fight back. This is what our constituents deserve from those of us in elected leadership. Go vote!”
 Speaking to reporters at a campaign stop in Sterling Heights earlier on Saturday, El-Sayed said his team had no involvement in the ad, adding: “I do not agree with the contents of that ad.”
 The ad, which blamed the high cost of living in Michigan on US aid to Israel, reopened a rift between the two Democrats who waged a sometimes contentious primary election battle, particularly over Israel. Stevens pressured El-Sayed on Friday to denounce the ad. El-Sayed responded in a statement Friday night that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.”
 “I just really don’t think any of this matters,” he told reporters Saturday, arguing that voters are more concerned with the cost of living than the dispute between the two Democrats.

 New NBC News poll finds voters want change, favor Democrats nationally
 By Ariel Edwards-Levy 
 Voters fill out their ballots at an early voting location in Minneapolis, on October 28. 
 Stephen Maturen/Getty Images 
 Amid widespread economic dissatisfaction and a desire for change, registered voters nationally say, 52% to 45%, that they’d prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress to one controlled by Republicans, an NBC News poll released Sunday finds.
 NBC’s findings echo the dynamics seen in national polling throughout most of this midterm campaign season. President Donald Trump’s approval rating is well underwater: 40% among registered voters in the NBC poll, and 34% among the broader public in CNN’s Poll of Polls average .
 Half of voters in the NBC poll say they’d like to see a great deal of change in the way Trump has been leading the country. Nearly half call cost-of-living concerns one of the top two issues facing the country. And the 51% who say they’re dissatisfied with their own personal financial situation marks a record high in NBC’s polling.
 At the same time, views of both political parties are net negative. And voters who’d rather see Democrats take control of Congress are roughly as likely to say that their preference is borne out of anti-Republican sentiment (48%) as they are to say it’s primarily out of support for the Democrats (51%) — a shift from 2018.
 The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters from October 28-30, using a combination of live telephone interviews and online surveys sent via text message. Results among the full sample have a margin of sampling error of +/-3.1 percentage points.

 Sullivan: Alleged duplicate candidate plot shows Peltola's "disdain" for Alaskans
 By Logan Schiciano 
 Sen. Dan Sullivan speaks at a campaign rally on October 5, in Fairbanks, Alaska. 
 Jacquelyn Martin/Pool/Getty Images/File 
 Alaska GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan slammed the campaign of his Democratic opponent Mary Peltola over its alleged involvement in recruiting another man named Dan Sullivan to run for Senate. But the incumbent senator did not say during an interview on CNN’s “State of the Union” that aired this morning whether the alleged actions constituted a crime, as many other Republicans, including President Donald Trump, have suggested.
 “I’ll let the lawyers figure that out,” Sullivan said told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “Whether or not this is legal or not, and I think you know there’s some good arguments on both sides… the key thing I’m focused on is looking at Peltola and her team — and the Democrats in DC, and how they treat Alaskans with disdain.”
 Sullivan floated a more than 150-year-old law, which was originally passed to combat the Ku Klux Klan, as a possible legal argument implicating Peltola’s campaign. The statute says it is illegal for any two people to conspire to deprive anyone of their constitutional rights, including the right to vote.
 Trump in recent days has called for Peltola, as well as the other Dan Sullivan, to be prosecuted .
 Sen. Sullivan did not directly address whether his campaign has evidence that Peltola knew about the alleged plan. Instead, he frequently referenced last week’s New York Times ’ report which, quoting Peltola’s former campaign manager, says the former Alaska congresswoman “definitely aware,” but not directly involved in the project.
 Despite all the attention the controversy has received, the senator said that the other Sullivan’s inclusion on the ballot may still confuse some Alaskans.
 “I’m sure I’m going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery,” he said.
 Some context: In Alaska’s Senate primary in August, the other Sullivan received 2.4% of the vote .
 He seemed to do better in Democratic-leaning precincts, suggesting he got support from Democratic-leaning voters who wanted him to advance, but who may ultimately vote for Peltola in the general election.

 Sen. Dan Sullivan says he will accept election results of Alaska Senate race 
 1:34
 Incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan says he will accept the outcome of his Senate race in Alaska, even if he loses, amid the controversy surrounding an alleged Democratic plot to recruit another man named Dan Sullivan as a spoiler candidate.
 When asked by CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union” in an interview that aired this morning if he will only accept the results if he wins, Sullivan said, “No, I’m going to accept the election results.”
 The senator’s comments come as Alaska’s GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy has launched an investigation into whether Democrats sought to confuse voters, and said last week that if the probe finds “wrongdoing,” then certification of the Senate race results could be “stopped or changed.”
 The Justice Department has launched a similar probe, which accelerated after the New York Times published a report last week detailing the plan and the alleged involvement of Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign.
 Meanwhile, others, including Republican Sen. Tim Sheehy, have said Peltola should not be seated if she wins the election.
 Despite Sullivan’s commitment to accepting the results, he concluded the interview by saying, “To all the Alaskans out there, get out there and vote. Don’t let this election be stolen.”
